<reason>Both sides argued well, but B built the cleaner decision path. B correctly anchored the motion's low bar ("hard to justify," not prohibited) and supplied a discriminating criterion — harm proportionate to benefit reaching past the buyer's own sensation — that acquits most of A's slippery-slope list while convicting the worst-ratio case. B also pressed a genuine fork (trivial enough to be climatically negligible vs. large enough to bend cost curves) and supported it with the plausible, largely unanswered structural point that reusable heavy launch was financed by satellite constellations and government payloads, not eleven-minute suborbital joyrides. A's reply — "two different scales," industrial thickening at "tens of flights a year" — was honest and non-fabricated, but B's rejoinder that such a cadence bends no cost curve and launches no climate satellite left A's spillover benefit thin precisely where A needed it. A's best work was the sequential-veto reframe and the counterfactual ("the fare was never becoming wells"), and A's pressure questions were sharp and productive. But B defused the "other luxuries already run" line by biting the bullet on private jets and polar cruises, which converted A's parity argument into a concession that the standard exists. A then had to answer that unresolved climate and poverty make no expensive private indulgence harder to justify, which B framed effectively as an amnesty that abolishes the question rather than answering it. A's counter that B's test also condemns beaches and concerts was a real hit, but B's distributed-benefit reply was plausible enough to survive. B's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost, and its closing slightly overstates A's answer by dropping the "merely because" qualifier, but neither offsets the edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's fork in Rebuttal 1 — tourism cannot be simultaneously too rare to matter climatically and large enough to amortize reusable vehicles — combined with the point that suborbital joyride hardware was not what paid for orbital reusable launch. A's "two different scales / tens of flights a year" answer was direct but let B land the closing counter that such a cadence delivers no industrial benefit, shrinking A's public-benefit case to match the emissions.</best_rebuttal>
